# Repair the offline PlanB64 forwarding tool

The software forwarding team needs a safe, reproducible FIB compiler and lookup tool. Its experimental interval implementation confuses prefix boundaries with winning routes and loses small tables and partial batches. Complete `/work/submit` so `make -C /work/submit` produces `/work/submit/planb64`.

This task is inspired by PlanB's reduction of longest-prefix matching (LPM) to predecessor search over disjoint intervals. The starter is an independently written teaching implementation, not the authors' artifact. You may replace its internals. Correct alternative data structures are accepted. There is no throughput ranking and no requirement to reproduce the paper's performance. All operation must work offline on an x86-64 CPU without AVX-512; optional SIMD must have a safe fallback.

## Deliverable and commands

Submit the complete source tree in `/work/submit`, including a Makefile. Use C++17 and the installed standard library and system headers only. The verifier copies only this directory into a fresh environment. It removes prebuilt binaries and runs `make clean` followed by `make`, with `CXX=g++` and externally supplied `CXXFLAGS`. Your build must honor those flags and produce `planb64`. Do not require generated files outside the tree, symlinks, network access, additional packages, or changes to the operating system. Public examples in `/work/examples` are for local checks and are not submitted.

The executable has exactly these interfaces (paths are positional):

```text
planb64 build FIB IMAGE
planb64 lookup IMAGE TRACE scalar
planb64 lookup IMAGE TRACE batch BATCH_SIZE
```

`build` writes the compiled image to `IMAGE` and writes nothing to stdout. `lookup` reads an image independently of the original FIB and prints one line per trace record, in original order:

```text
NEXT_HOP PREFIX_LENGTH
```

Use `-1 -1` for no match; a valid default route reports its actual next hop and length `0`. Numeric fields in successful output are unpadded decimal. Both lookup modes have identical semantics. `BATCH_SIZE` must be a nonempty string of ASCII decimal digits (`0` through `9`) denoting a value from 1 through 256. Leading zeros are allowed (for example, `003` means 3); signs, embedded whitespace, and any other characters are invalid. Sizes that do not divide the trace length are valid. Empty traces produce no lines. Scalar and batch are selectable execution interfaces; any correct implementation within the resource limits is accepted.

## FIB and LPM semantics

FIB files contain zero or more records, one per nonblank line:

```text
IPV6_ADDRESS/PREFIX_LENGTH NEXT_HOP
```

An address must be accepted by Linux `inet_pton(AF_INET6, ...)`: compressed and uppercase forms and IPv4-embedded IPv6 are allowed; IPv4-only addresses, zone IDs, and CIDR suffixes on trace addresses are not. The prefix length is decimal digits denoting a value from **0 through 64 inclusive**. Next hops are decimal digits denoting an unsigned 32-bit value, including zero and 4294967295. Leading zeros in input decimal fields are allowed. Signs, overflow, extra tokens, and comments are invalid.

Normalize every FIB prefix by clearing its host bits, including the lower 64 bits. Two records that normalize to the same network and prefix length are an error, even if the next hop is identical. Different lengths and overlapping networks are valid. For each query, choose the matching normalized prefix with greatest length, independently of FIB order. The supported prefix bound means the upper 64 address bits determine the answer; the lower 64 bits must still be parsed and validated. `/65` through `/128` are errors, not silently skipped and not approximated. A missing default route does not create one.

Trace files contain one IPv6 address per nonblank line. FIB and trace records allow spaces, tabs, and carriage returns as whitespace. Blank lines are ignored. There are no comments. An optional final newline is allowed. Inputs are ASCII text.

## Canonical interval image

Compile the function from unsigned 64-bit upper-address key to the pair `(NEXT_HOP, PREFIX_LENGTH)`. The image contains its **minimal change-point representation** covering every key from 0 through 2^64-1. The first key is always zero. Each later key occurs exactly where the pair changes from its predecessor key. Thus adjacent rows must have different pairs. Keep a boundary when the winning prefix length changes even if the next hop stays the same. Do not keep redundant prefix endpoints. No explicit end key or sentinel past 2^64-1 is stored.

The image format is ASCII, one nonempty line per record, with a final newline:

```text
PLANB64 1
ROW_COUNT
START_HEX NEXT_HOP PREFIX_LENGTH
...
```

`START_HEX` is exactly 16 lowercase hexadecimal digits representing an unsigned 64-bit upper-address key. Rows are strictly increasing. The row count is from 1 through 400001 and must equal the number of rows. Numeric fields are unpadded decimal; the only negative fields are the paired no-match values `-1 -1`. Matched rows have next hop 0..4294967295 and length 0..64. Use exactly one ASCII space between fields, no leading/trailing spaces, no blank lines, and no extra records. A compiler must emit this exact canonical serialization, independent of FIB order.

The reader must reject malformed images: wrong header/version, bad count or count mismatch, invalid hex or decimal fields, unordered/duplicate keys, a first key other than zero, invalid pair ranges or one-sided no-match, equal adjacent pairs, missing final newline, extra records, or noncanonical spacing/number spellings. Apart from these structural rules, an image is a complete standalone interval function; the reader must not infer an unavailable source FIB or impose extra route-consistency rules.

For an empty FIB the complete image is:

```text
PLANB64 1
1
0000000000000000 -1 -1
```

## Errors and limits

On success, return exit status 0 and write no stderr. On invalid arguments, malformed input, an unsupported prefix length, a duplicate normalized prefix, or a file I/O failure, return **2**, write no stdout, and write a nonempty stderr message beginning `ERROR:`. The text after that prefix is unrestricted. Validate the complete image and trace before printing answers. For a failed build, leave an existing destination unchanged and do not create a new destination. Input and output paths are distinct regular-file paths in writable directories; concurrent file replacement, special files, broken pipes, and injected OS failures are outside the test domain.

Supported limits per invocation are 200000 FIB records and 1000000 trace records, with lines at most 256 bytes. An image contains at most 400001 rows. Inputs exceeding these limits may be rejected with the same error behavior. Normal optimized builds run with one CPU, a 512 MiB address-space limit, and a generous 30-second wall limit per invocation. Smaller safety cases are also compiled with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and must finish without diagnostics; sanitizer runs have a 60-second limit and no address-space cap because ASan reserves virtual memory. Compilation has 120 seconds and 1 GiB. These are operational safety limits, not a latency or throughput score. Use an index rather than scanning the entire FIB for every query.

The following additional resource bounds apply to the complete invocation, including startup, input validation, empty inputs, and all descendants:

- For each executable invocation, aggregate stdout is capped at 32 MiB and aggregate stderr at 1 MiB. Caps count raw bytes before decoding, separately for each stream, across the initial process and its descendants. Here 1 MiB is 1048576 bytes. These caps do not relax the required output format or the requirement for empty stderr on success. The longest legal answer line is 14 bytes, so even 1000000 answers need at most 14000000 stdout bytes.
- Each complete build command (`make clean` or `make`) has an 8 MiB raw-byte cap on stdout and a separate 8 MiB cap on stderr, aggregated over the build command and its descendants.
- An executable invocation or build command may have at most 64 live Linux tasks at once over its entire process tree. Each thread counts as one task, including the initial main thread and every thread in every descendant process. This is a concurrent bound, not a cumulative limit on tasks created during the command.
- Every candidate or build process has both soft and hard `RLIMIT_NOFILE` set to 256: newly allocated file-descriptor numbers must be below 256. Standard streams use descriptors 0, 1, and 2; the runner closes other inherited descriptors before launch. This is the kernel descriptor-number limit, rather than a separate count of open files.

Time limits begin at command launch and include startup, parsing, index construction, and output. Exceeding any resource bound may terminate the command and fails that invocation; producing an `ERROR:` message is not required after resource-limit exhaustion. The 30-second and 60-second executable budgets and 120-second compilation budget above are unchanged by these additional bounds.

```sh
make -C /work/submit
/work/submit/planb64 build /work/examples/fib.txt /work/example.idx
cmp /work/example.idx /work/examples/expected.idx
/work/submit/planb64 lookup /work/example.idx /work/examples/trace.txt scalar
/work/submit/planb64 lookup /work/example.idx /work/examples/trace.txt batch 3
/work/submit/planb64 lookup /work/example.idx /work/examples/trace.txt batch 003
```

All lookup outputs must match `/work/examples/expected.txt`. The examples exercise only a small portion of the contract; complete the tool for the full input domain above.


Local trial profile (overrides conflicting execution-resource statements in the original task): offline Linux x86-64; no network or Unix sockets, System V IPC, background processes across tool calls, namespace operations, or signalling other processes. Only files in /work/submit are transferred to the grader; no symlinks, hardlinks, special files, or more than 10000 entries or 256 MiB total in that directory. Maximum file size is 64 MiB. Agent shell tool: at most two assigned CPUs, 180 seconds wall per call, 2 GiB virtual memory per process, 64 processes/threads per UID, 256 file descriptors, maximum output 2 MiB; CPU limit 180 seconds per process. The complete agent gets 100 model calls and 4 hours wall time; each tool call starts a fresh shell and all surviving background processes are stopped. The private evaluator runs the complete optimized functional suite including its largest cases, but does not run AddressSanitizer or UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer in this local trial. It denies all sockets and limits each file to 64 MiB. Writable storage has no hard aggregate quota: a sampled 1 GiB / 50000-entry emergency brake may terminate the run as infrastructure error, and the final submission has its own limits; use this profile consistently across models. Grading is binary; grader or interface errors do not produce a score.

When finished run exactly: echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT
